story.intro: ConnectAid is a mobile healthcare prototype for consultations, medicines, lab tests and health records. In our eight-week, five-person project, I built the core Figma design system and coordinated remote usability testing. We later reviewed parts of the design again in October 2026.

blocks.text: ConnectAid brings booking consultations, finding medicines and lab tests, and returning to health records into one app prototype. Home is the starting point for care services; Records stays in the main navigation for use after a visit.

blocks.text: What testing changed
Remote usability testing with six participants covered 11 scripted tasks. Nine documented findings led to six refinements across navigation, data entry and task controls.

items.title: Finding services
items.body: More visible navigation and another route to the lab-test listing.

items.title: Entering details
items.body: Revised date entry and the ability to search by doctor specialty.

items.title: Moving through tasks
items.body: A repositioned cart and lighter side-panel content in the prototype.

blocks.text: All screens use sample content. The outcome is a designed and tested prototype, not a launched healthcare service; the Usability testing chapter shows what we changed and what remains unverified.

People arranging care for themselves or a family member faced three questions: can this need be handled online, who can I trust, and where will my prescriptions and reports go afterwards? Our survey and interviews surfaced concerns about virtual care, unfamiliar doctors and sharing medical information. The prototype connects care options, booking details and records so those decisions can be made in one place.

We designed for adults arranging their own or a family member’s care. Independent use by older adults and use in languages other than English were design goals, rather than audiences established by our testing.
The four care tasks

items.title: Consultations
items.body: Book online and in-clinic visits.

items.title: Medicines
items.body: Order medicines.

items.title: Lab tests
items.body: Find tests and scans.

items.title: Health records
items.body: Return to prescriptions and reports.

blocks.text: We organised consultations, medicines and lab tests around Home, and kept health records in the main navigation. The goal was to help people book care for themselves or a family member and access their records afterwards.
Three priorities

items.title: Clear booking details
items.body: Make the patient, appointment and total fee clear before confirmation.

items.title: Records after the visit
items.body: Keep prescriptions and reports easy to find.

items.title: Language choice
items.body: Keep language switching available beyond initial setup.

blocks.text: We used a survey, interviews and a review of four healthcare apps to understand how people chose care and what concerned them about online consultations.

items.title: Survey · 189 submissions
items.body: Healthcare habits, previous telemedicine use and concerns. Of these, 114 were aged 21–30 and none were over 60; answers about older relatives were indirect.

items.title: Interviews · 5 documented
items.body: How people chose doctors, involved family and described their difficulties. The case records themes, but does not establish the interviewees’ age, language or digital-confidence coverage.

items.title: Competitive review · Four apps
items.body: Navigation, screen content, service discovery and doctor information.

items.title: Later usability study · 6 participants
items.body: Remote, moderated use of our prototype across 11 tasks. This is a separate sample from discovery; its demographic coverage is not documented here.

blocks.text: Previous use and concerns
Before testing our prototype, 103 of 189 survey submissions (54.5%) selected “I have never used telemedicine”.

items.title: Limits of virtual care · 64.0%
items.body: 121 of 189 submissions selected concern about medical issues that cannot be solved virtually.

items.title: Missing medical equipment · 47.1%
items.body: 89 of 189 submissions selected the absence of equipment for taking readings.

items.title: Trust in unfamiliar doctors · 31.2%
items.body: 59 of 189 submissions selected this concern.

items.title: Data privacy · 27.0%
items.body: 51 of 189 submissions selected this concern.

blocks.text: The survey allowed multiple selections. One submission selected both “never used” and a usage option. Two written “No” answers were not added to the 103 selections.
What the interviews added

items.title: Remote care was not always called telemedicine
items.body: Some people described contacting doctors through WhatsApp and calls without identifying this as telemedicine.

items.title: Familiar doctors influenced trust
items.body: Interview notes described a preference for known doctors and their referrals to specialists.

items.title: Sharing records raised privacy concerns
items.body: People saw value in sharing medical information but were concerned about sharing it online.

blocks.text: From findings to screens

items.title: Virtual care had limits → keep care options visible
items.body: With 121 of 189 submissions concerned about issues that cannot be handled virtually, we kept clinic and lab routes alongside online consultations on Home.

items.title: Unfamiliar doctors raised concern → show details before booking
items.body: Interviewees valued known doctors and referrals. We showed specialty, experience, ratings and patient stories before confirmation so people had information to consider before committing.

blocks.text: These choices respond to the research. We did not measure whether they changed trust or increased telemedicine use.

The research pointed to three needs: useful doctor information before booking, follow-up guidance after a visit, and easy access to prescriptions and reports. We grouped the research notes, created two personas and mapped a planned care journey to turn these needs into design priorities.
The patterns behind the priorities

The affinity map groups research notes and proposed features into 12 topics. Booking was only one part of the activity: reports from a lab could be needed at a follow-up, and prescriptions needed to remain available after the consultation.

visual.alt: Original affinity board grouping notes and ideas around doctor information, medicines, consultations, profiles, waiting, search, lab tests and support.
visual.caption: Original team synthesis board · The notes include research interpretation and ideas explored, rather than a list of delivered features.

blocks.text: Two personas to guide decisions
We used two fictional personas to consider independence, language preference and time constraints. Their names and profiles are synthesised design tools, not identified research participants.

items.title: Shekhar Gupta · 73 · Retired librarian · Dehradun
items.body: Wants to manage regular care independently: book appointments, find prescriptions and access reports from regular tests. Design focus: clear booking steps and records that are easy to find. The survey contained no respondents over 60, so this older-adult profile had indirect support.

items.title: Rajesh Patel · 42 · Businessman · Jamnagar
items.body: Needs to fit care around a busy workday. Comfortable with Gujarati and Hindi, with limited English. Design focus: simple booking steps, clear labels and an accessible language choice.

blocks.text: The planned care journey
The planned journey follows a consultation into lab tests and a follow-up, rather than ending at the first booking.

items: Create a profile: add personal details and medical history.
Book a doctor: review the doctor, choose a time and confirm.
Attend the consultation: discuss symptoms, treatment and any required tests.
Complete tests: choose a lab, complete the tests and get reports.
Follow up: share reports and discuss the next steps.

visual.alt: Planned care journey across profile creation, consultation scheduling, consulting a doctor, booking lab tests and a follow-up, with tasks, emotions and opportunities.
visual.caption: Original team journey map · A planned experience, not an observed end-to-end service journey.

blocks.text: That connection shaped the navigation: Home starts a new care task, while Records remains a main destination for returning to earlier information. The journey map helped us connect those tasks instead of designing each service as an isolated flow.

We prioritised clear doctor information, language choice, records and the routes between care tasks. During an adapted five-day sprint, we used questions, team voting and an impact–effort matrix to decide what to prototype.
Questions the sprint focused on
We wrote How might we questions and used team voting to focus the sprint. The highlighted questions concerned medicine information, organised records, independent use, language and access needs.

visual.alt: Original How might we board with highlighted questions and team votes about medicine information, records, independent use, access and language.
visual.caption: Original sprint board · Stars highlight questions; red dots record team votes.

blocks.text: Compare value with effort

We used an impact–effort matrix to compare the value of ideas with the work needed to prototype them. The positions were team estimates. Appointment booking and doctor information were relatively direct to explore; language support, records and delivery involved a wider set of screens and service questions.

items.title: Quick wins · Higher impact, lower effort
items.body: Appointment scheduling, doctor reviews and medicine reminders.

items.title: Major projects · Higher impact, higher effort
items.body: Language switching, profiles and medical records, and medicine delivery.

items.title: Smaller additions · Lower impact, lower effort
items.body: A discussion forum and referral benefits.

items.title: More effort, less impact
items.body: Smart-device integration.

visual.alt: Original impact–effort matrix sorting ideas into quick wins, major projects, fill-ins and higher-effort tasks.
visual.caption: Original team planning board · Estimates used to compare prototype priorities.

blocks.text: The routes selected for prototyping

items.title: Consultations
items.body: Home, then doctor information, then booking review.

items.title: Lab tests
items.body: Home, then tests and scans.

items.title: Records
items.body: Open Records, then Prescriptions.

blocks.text: We took consultation, lab and record routes into the sketches. The matrix also kept wider ideas visible without implying that every idea—such as smart-device integration or a discussion forum—was delivered in the prototype.

We sketched alternatives for Home and the main care tasks, compared them as a team, then connected selected ideas into storyboards. Crazy 8s—a rapid sketching exercise—helped us explore several layouts before choosing a direction.

We ran remote, moderated sessions with six participants across 11 scripted tasks. Tasks covered setup, language switching, consultations, medicines, lab tests, prescriptions and the SOS concept. The study documented nine findings and led to six design refinements.
The nine documented findings

items: Date-of-birth entry was difficult with the calendar.
Participants overlooked the bottom navigation.
Participants preferred English and were reluctant to switch languages in these sessions.
A slowly loading side panel prompted repeated, unintended clicks.
The list of available lab tests was hard to find.
Adding items to the cart required repeated scrolling.
Participants tried searching by doctor specialty instead of following the intended category route.
Prescription details were difficult to reach when the bottom navigation was overlooked.
Participants had trouble finding the list of lab-test bookings.

visual.alt: Original usability findings board with nine notes on date input, navigation, language, side-panel delay, lab discovery, cart, specialty search, prescriptions and bookings.
visual.caption: Original nine-finding summary · A historical study artifact, not evidence that all issues were resolved.

blocks.text: Six refinements

blocks.before: Date of birth: participants had difficulty entering a birth date with the calendar.
blocks.after: We replaced calendar browsing with separate day, month and year selection, so people could enter the date they already knew without browsing month by month.
blocks.note: Date-entry control → separate values for a known date. The before/after artifact below shows the change; no comparative completion-time result was recorded.

blocks.before: Specialty search: participants searched for the doctor’s specialty rather than using the category route.
blocks.after: We enabled search by specialty while retaining category browsing. This supported the terms participants tried instead of requiring them to follow our chosen category route.
blocks.note: Doctor discovery → search and browsing both remain available. This follows the route participants actually tried; keeping both means their specialty labels and destinations must agree.

visual.alt: Original before-and-after evidence for date-of-birth controls and the additional doctor-specialty search route.
visual.caption: Original refinement evidence · Date entry and specialty search.

blocks.before: Lab-test discovery: participants had trouble finding the list of tests.
blocks.after: We connected View all beside Popular Tests to the test listing, while retaining the main booking entry.
blocks.note: Lab services → View all and the main booking entry lead to the same listing. We added a route at the point people were already exploring tests.

blocks.before: Bottom navigation: participants overlooked the navigation and missed routes to records.
blocks.after: We made the active destination indicator more prominent.
blocks.note: Shared navigation → a stronger active state. The source artifact shows this visual change; prescription and booking-history retrieval still need a task check.

visual.alt: Original before-and-after evidence for a stronger active bottom-navigation indicator and a second route to lab-test listings.
visual.caption: Original refinement evidence · Navigation visibility and lab-test discovery.

items.title: Cart · Bring the control into view
items.body: Adding items required repeated scrolling. We repositioned the cart control to make it easier to reach.

items.title: Side panel · Reduce prototype delay
items.body: The panel responded slowly and prompted repeated clicks. We reduced the content beneath the overlay in the prototype. This addressed the Figma interaction, rather than demonstrating a production performance improvement.

blocks.text: These six changes trace the finding summary to a revised control or route. The available case records do not include verbatim task prompts, per-participant observations, device details or a definition of completion and assistance. We therefore report the issues and changes, rather than reconstructing a success rate or ranking them by an unknown frequency.
What the changes did not settle

A stronger navigation indicator is a visible design change, but it does not establish that people can now find prescriptions or lab-booking history. The source does not show a separate change for booking history. Those tasks still need to be checked.

Participants preferred English in these sessions. We kept language choice available, but this study does not establish how well the other language flows work. Some users informally reviewed the refinements; there was no comparable second study or measured improvement in task completion.

The high-fidelity screens focus on consultation review, lab-test discovery and prescription access. These exports include the later colour refinements. Names, clinician profiles, dates, offers, prices and prescription content are prototype examples.

blocks.after: Refined colour pair: white text on #005982 measures 7.63:1.

blocks.text: Proposed payment readiness

In the payment-readiness proposal, Confirm & Pay becomes available after a payment method is selected. The specimen separates the ₹1,000 clinic consultation and ₹49 service charge, for a total of ₹1,049. UPI is an illustrative option; the specimen does not process payments.

visual.alt: Approved payment-readiness specimen showing consultation and service charges, a total of 1,049 rupees, unselected UPI and an unavailable Confirm and Pay control.
visual.caption: Payment proposal · Static design; interaction not yet tested.

items.title: No method selected
items.body: Explain that a payment method is needed before continuing. Keep Confirm & Pay unavailable.

items.title: Method selected
items.body: Enable the next action while keeping the selected patient and total visible.

blocks.text: Both proposals address a decision before commitment: who the appointment is for and what must happen before payment. The next study should check whether people understand the selected patient, the total charge and when payment becomes available.

We delivered a tested healthcare prototype and made six refinements in response to the usability findings. The later review also improved selected colour pairs and proposed clearer patient and payment choices. We still need to test the revised tasks before claiming that they are easier to complete.

items.title: Support more than one starting point
items.body: Participants searched by specialty and looked for different routes to lab tests. Search and browsing should remain available with consistent labels and destinations.

items.title: Check accessibility before reuse
items.body: Shared components kept screens consistent, but the later review found low button contrast. Contrast and interaction states need checking when the components are defined.

items.title: Resolve the core before adding more
items.body: Booking and records need further testing before live waiting information or other integrations. Patient selection, total charges and access to records come first.

items.title: A revision still needs evidence
items.body: Testing led to six refinements and informal feedback followed, but improvement was not measured. Another study should include different levels of digital confidence.

blocks.text: Test the tasks that caused difficulty

First, compare the original and revised flows for date-of-birth entry, specialty search and lab-test discovery. Then check whether people can retrieve prescriptions and lab-booking history. Include people with lower digital confidence and different language preferences, rather than treating the first sessions as coverage of those needs.

items: Task completion
Time taken
Assistance needed

blocks.text: Use those results to decide which routes need another revision. Keep the proposed patient and payment changes in that next study before expanding into more services.

outcome.title: Current outcome
outcome.text: We built a healthcare prototype, tested it remotely with six people across 11 tasks, and made six refinements from nine findings. The revised tasks still need a comparable retest; no improvement in task completion or live service performance has been measured.
